brief.text:
THE PLAYER'S WORDS
Okay, can you make a incantation? That fires a fireball whenever I say Hot fireball

THE WHOLE PICTURE
When Steve says 'Hot fireball' in chat, a ghast fireball spawns just ahead of Steve's eyes and shoots forward in the exact direction Steve is looking, complete with a ghast shoot sound and a trail of smoke and flame particles, exploding and dealing damage when it strikes a block or mob.

WHAT THE PLAYER TAKES FOR GRANTED
The fireball moves straight along Steve's line of sight; it does not blow up instantly in Steve's face or hit Steve upon spawning; it detonates upon contact with solid blocks or entities; it is specifically bound to Steve's voice/incantation.

HOW IT IS CAST, AND FOR WHOM
Incantation: Steve says 'Hot fireball' (or close aliases like 'hot fireball') in chat.

DONE WHEN
- Incantation 'Hot fireball' is registered for Steve
- Steve saying 'Hot fireball' spawns a fireball travelling forward from Steve's eye line
- The fireball plays appropriate launch audio and effects
- The fireball collides with blocks or mobs and detonates without damaging Steve upon firing

runs.report: Done: I investigated Steve's voice latency and changed nothing. The capture and speech code runs on his PC in the Java client mod (`client-mod/`), so the box can't time it, and this shell can't run the Python measurement tools. From the repo's measured numbers, the mod's defaults give a median of 0.49 s from his last word to the line being ready: a 0.35 s Silero VAD pause, then Parakeet transcription and a roughly 35 ms Smart Turn score, which decides whether the line closes at once or waits up to 3 s. That probably accounts for most of his 0.6 s. On the box, a voice line waits at most 50 ms, action and conversational lines skip the batch wait, then Jev classifies it and the brain answers. The box log shows about 4 s from one of his lines to the AI's acknowledgement (06:20:33 to 06:20:37), so the server side is probably the bigger share, but Jev's and the brain's own times aren't measured here. The trade-offs: cutting the VAD pause to about 0.2 s saves roughly 0.15 s but risks splitting sentences, and needs a client rebuild on his PC; lowering the turn threshold to 0.35 (turn-1-mini) cuts off unfinished speech more often and doesn't clearly help; Moonshine tiny is faster but makes more errors than Parakeet (19.2% against 11.5% word errors for base). Recognition errors matter more than 0.6 s: his casts came through as "Hot fire bowl", "Tijum", "Hawfio" and "Destroying every bin". Skipping Jev for lines that match an incantation would save one API round-trip, at the cost of its context. Before any change, run `./gradlew speechTest` on his PC and time Jev and the brain from the box logs; any change to the client or the server waits for the brain's go-ahead.

Done, with a caveat: I could not run new benchmarks from this shell (it refuses Gradle, Java and Python measurement tools), so every number below comes from the repo's own reports, measured on the owner's PC on 2026-10-08 to 2026-10-10. The main finding is that the 0.6 s is not the main latency problem. A line closes at once when Smart Turn scores it finished, but on Kokoro-spoken game asks it scores 19% of finished asks unfinished, and those wait the full 3 s silence timeout, so the average is pulled up by about 0.6 s. Lowering the Smart Turn threshold to 0.3 cuts that wait to 15% but cuts off 35% of unfinished asks mid-sentence. Asking the model 0.6 s into the pause, rather than 0.2 s, cuts those waits from 5.4% to 1.5% on the public set, but adds 0.4 s to every line, which is a net loss. turn-1-mini is worse on both counts: it keeps 64% of game asks waiting at its chosen 0.35 threshold. On recognition, Parakeet TDT 110M (the current default) makes 11.5% word errors against Moonshine base's 19.2% on Minecraft-heavy speech, at similar size, speed and memory; the repo's hotwords option for Parakeet is experimental and was not benchmarked against the errors seen in the log ("Hot fire bowl", "Tijum", "Hawfio"). The cheapest accuracy fix is the incantation aliases the keyword spotter already supports. Streaming recognition (partial text during speech, so nothing is left to transcribe after the pause) and a sherpa streaming model are plausible next steps, but they are not in the repo and would need a sttCompare run before any recommendation. Server-side time (the Jev filter, then the brain) is also unmeasured: the box logs show about 4 s from one of his lines to the AI's acknowledgement. My recommendation: keep Parakeet and Smart Turn at 0.5, measure the hotwords and a streaming model with `./gradlew sttCompare` and `micCheck` on the owner's PC, and time Jev and the brain from the box logs before changing any threshold. No changes were made to the game or the code.

Failed: I could not do the web research. This session has no web search or fetch tool, and the shell refuses curl and every other network program, so I have no sources to cite and I made no claims about outside products or prices. Nothing on the server or in the repo was changed.

What the repo does establish, without outside sources: transcription runs on each player's own PC, and no audio leaves it (client-mod README). So multiplayer scaling does not load the box for speech: each player adds only their text lines to the bridge, which Jev and the brain then handle. The box-side cost per voice line is therefore the text path, and I measured nothing there except the 4 s gap from one line to the AI's acknowledgement in the logs. Hosted-model costs, custom-training gains and game-side streaming implementations would need the web research, which needs a session with web access. The brain should either run that research with a web-capable implementer or give me a web tool and a new task. The repo's own measured figures from the previous report still stand as the only evidence.

brief.text:
THE PLAYER'S WORDS
Make a black hole that eats all the blocks around it.

THE WHOLE PICTURE
Steve throws an item named Black Hole Core. Where it lands or activates in mid-air, a dense swirling sphere of dark portal, smoke, and reverse-portal particles forms with an ominous hum. Over several seconds, nearby blocks in a spherical radius (around 6 blocks) are broken into falling block entities, dragged violently toward the center point, and deleted upon touch.
